profile.a: The author, writing a letter to the editor for Macroeconomics.
Readers of The Guardian and, through them, UK financial regulators.
Whether AI chatbots giving personal financial advice are a helpful tool or a dangerous shortcut, and what regulators should do.
Responds to a Guardian test published on 14 June 2025 and a Bank of England warning reported on 9 April 2025; handed in on 23 June 2025.
The UK (Bank of England) and the EU (European Securities and Markets Authority).

Experts found ChatGPT's mortgage advice 'not even close' to qualified advice and its pension answers contained basic errors such as the wrong state pension age, delivered with confidence consumers may not question.
A 298-word argument moving from the test evidence, to the risk for consumers, to the risk for markets, to a specific request to regulators.

facts.what: Experts' verdict on ChatGPT pension guidance
Bank of England warning on AI and market manipulation

charts.title: How the experts rated ChatGPT's advice
charts.takeaway: Quality falls as the product gets more complex and personal. Mortgages, where borrower criteria and deal structures matter most, is where the chatbot failed outright.
charts.source: Page 159. The scale orders the experts' quoted verdicts; it is not a score from the article.

charts.title: How the letter builds its case

items.title: The evidence
items.text: Expert reviewers find pension advice usable, insurance generic and mortgages unfit.

items.title: The consumer risk
items.text: Incomplete answers given with confidence can push people into the wrong products.

items.title: The system risk
items.text: The Bank of England warns AI trading could exploit weaknesses and trigger volatility.

items.title: The rules
items.text: The Bank of England and ESMA say AI must sit within existing oversight and transparency rules.

items.title: The ask
items.text: Decide whether AI platforms giving financial guidance need authorisation, and require clear disclaimers.

charts.takeaway: Step three is the weak link: it moves from a consumer chatbot to institutional trading, two different risks.

charts.title: Helpful tool or dangerous shortcut

left.title: Helpful
items: A useful starting point (The Guardian's own conclusion)
Free access for people who cannot afford an adviser (not raised in the letter)

right.title: Dangerous
items: Ignores borrower criteria and alternative deal structures
Basic factual errors, e.g. state pension age

charts.takeaway: The letter argues only the right-hand side; the access argument on the left is the main counter-case it leaves unanswered.
